title: Control Flow
summary: Make decisions with if, else and switch, repeat work with for, foreach, while and do loops, and control loops with break and continue.
introduction: Programs become useful when they react to data: charge shipping only above a threshold, retry until a download succeeds, print every item in a list. C# offers the familiar if/else and loops of the C family, a switch statement that refuses to fall through by accident, and a compact switch expression that returns a value. This lesson works through each construct with a small program and its output, so you can see exactly which branch runs and how many times a loop body executes.
learningObjectives: Choose between if/else, a switch statement and a switch expression
Write for, foreach, while and do loops and know when each fits
Exit or skip loop iterations with break and continue

blocks.text: `if` tests a `bool` expression and runs its block when the expression is `true`. Unlike JavaScript or Python, C# does not treat numbers or strings as "truthy": the condition must be an actual `bool`, so `if (count)` is a compile error and you write `if (count > 0)`. Chain alternatives with `else if` and finish with `else` for the remaining cases.

Only the first matching branch runs, which is why `Pleasant` is printed although 23 is also not below 20. The last two lines use the **conditional operator** `condition ? a : b`, a one-line `if`/`else` that produces a value. Combine conditions with the operators below; `&&` and `||` stop evaluating as soon as the answer is known, so `x != null && x.Length > 0` is safe.

rows: equal, not equal (for strings this compares the characters)

blocks.text: When one value is compared against many constants, `switch` reads better than a ladder of `else if`. Each `case` section must end with `break` (or `return` or `throw`): C# does not let execution fall through into the next section by accident, although several labels may share one section, as `Saturday` and `Sunday` do here.

Since C# 8 a `switch` can also be an **expression** that produces a value. There are no `case` or `break` keywords: each arm is `pattern => result`, `_` is the catch-all, and arms may use relational patterns such as `>= 500` or combine constants with `or`. Because it is an expression you can assign it, return it or pass it to a method directly.

Arms are tested top to bottom, so `Grade(91)` stops at the first arm. The compiler warns when the arms do not cover every possible value, and a value that no arm matches throws a `SwitchExpressionException` at runtime. The [pattern matching lesson](/tutorials/csharp/properties-records) shows the richer patterns these arms accept.

C# has four loops. `for` is for counting, `foreach` walks through every element of a collection, `while` repeats while a condition holds (possibly zero times) and `do`/`while` runs its body at least once before checking.

blocks.text: The `for` header has three parts separated by semicolons: initialise `i`, test `i <= 3` before each iteration, and update `i++` after each one. Prefer `foreach` whenever you only need the elements and do not care about the index; it works with arrays, lists, dictionaries, strings and anything else that is enumerable.
`break` leaves the loop immediately; `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one. Both apply to the innermost loop only.

Loops nest freely. The inner loop runs to completion for every single iteration of the outer loop, so two loops of three produce nine values. The `,3` inside the braces right-aligns each number in a field three characters wide.

blocks.title: Off-by-one and infinite loops
blocks.text: `for (int i = 0; i <= items.Length; i++)` visits one index too many and throws `IndexOutOfRangeException` on the last iteration; arrays start at 0, so the test must be `i < items.Length`. A `while` loop whose body never changes the condition runs forever: make sure something inside the loop moves towards the exit.

blocks.title: Braces are optional, but safer
blocks.text: `if (x > 0) Console.WriteLine(x);` is legal without braces, but only that one statement belongs to the `if`. Adding a second indented line later is a classic bug, because it runs unconditionally. Many teams always write the braces.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: The loop adds 0, 1 and 2 to `total`. When `i` reaches 3 the `break` leaves the loop before anything else is added, so the result is 3.

questions.question: In a C# switch statement, execution silently falls through from one case section to the next when you omit break.
questions.explanation: Omitting `break` is a compile error (CS0163), not silent fall-through. Only empty labels such as `case 1: case 2:` may stack on one section.
